nodes.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
nodes.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
nodes.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

nodes.scope_note: A Debate entry with five components, each with its own strands: the transition debate; the Brenner debate and political Marxism; explaining industrialisation; the Great Divergence; slavery and capitalism. It gathers exchanges; each author's own contribution stays on the field entries, whose related strands are not moved: marx/transition, economic/marxist, economic/household_demand, economic/wrigley_growth, economic/regional_divergence, economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute (the Huang–Pomeranz exchange), economic/slavery_productivity_exchange, economic/empire, global/comparison, global/reciprocal_comparison_resources, global/protoindustry_trade_limits, consumption/household_labor, technology/invention_adoption, demography/aggregate_population, dependency/worldsystems, atlantic/earlier and quant/slavery_debate. Existing person entries (Dobb, Hilton, Williams, Pomeranz, Huang, Hall) keep their own relations; the new person entries are Brenner and Wood. Readings are recorded per source, many through publisher excerpts, abstracts, Cambridge Core chapter openings or reviewers; unread books are given only as named readers report them. Quotations from another copy of The Brenner Debate (1985) were withdrawn before drafting. The 'California School' is a readers' label, attributed by Frank (2001) and Vries (2009) to Goldstone. Toynbee (1884) is a dated precursor, not a start. Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries, Wong, Allen and Beckert are roster rows here; person entries for them are a later step.

representative_people.context: Defined feudalism by 'the relations between the direct producer and his overlord' and answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950, pp. 158, 160). Brenner acknowledged a 'great debt' to him (1977).

representative_people.context: Feudalism as 'a system of production for use', dissolved by 'causes external to the system', chiefly trade (1950, pp. 136, 141), offered as a correction from within: 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct' (p. 142). Brenner (1977) traced Wallerstein's and Frank's 'neo-Smithian' Marxism back to him.

Co-author with Postan of the 1978 reply to Brenner.

Co-author with Croot of the 1978 comparison of France and England.

Bohemia as 'a variant case' in Brenner's comparison (1979, p. 192).

In his own account (1974, read in part), a world-economy's division of labour defines the unit of analysis, with external arenas distinguished from internal exchange, and coerced labour can belong to capitalism. Brenner's 1977 critique treated the world-system as an outgrowth of Sweezy's position.

Target of Brenner's 1977 critique, credited with breaking stage theory; ReOrient (1998) put Asia at the centre of the early modern world economy, was announced to debate Landes (December 1998) and reviewed Pomeranz as 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution' (2001).
representative_people.works: Development of underdevelopment (1966–); ReOrient (1998); JAS review (2001)

representative_people.context: Called Wood's political Marxism 'little more than a sociology of domination' while finding Brenner's 1977 critique 'a valuable corrective' (1990).
Brenner 'take[s] up Dobb's argument, but simplif[ies] it' (1989); debated Brenner in London (2004).
Criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal, drawing on Blaut (2001).
His posthumous lectures defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations' and found that it produced 'wealth without producing well-being' (1884).

representative_people.context: With Harley, revised British output growth downward while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992, abstract); his 1985 book is known here through Berg and Hudson.

representative_people.context: Co-author of the 1992 restatement; reviewing Mokyr (2010), doubted whether 'causation from Enlightenment … actually existed'.

Co-author with Berg of the 1992 rehabilitation of the Industrial Revolution.

Questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime (1988; 2013; 2016). Berg and Hudson criticised the aggregative demography he built with Schofield (1990).
representative_people.works: Continuity, Chance and Change (1988); "Energy and the English Industrial Revolution" (2013); The Path to Sustained Growth (2016)

representative_people.context: Named market-oriented rural industry 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper' (1972) and later 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); Stone credited him, 'so far as I can discover', as 'the originator of the word and idea of proto-industrialization'.
With Medick and Schlumbohm, rural industry 'in the genesis of capitalism' (1977; English 1981). Contents read only.
Göttingen collaborator on the proto-industrial family economy (1976), chapter 2 of the 1977 book. Body unread.
Third Göttingen co-author of Industrialisierung vor der Industrialisierung (1977).

Proposed the 'industrious revolution' as a household-level, demand-side change preceding the supply-side Industrial Revolution, in response to the Crafts–Harley revision (1994); Pomeranz used it for Chinese households (2000). Van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009) found consumption made 'a new deus ex machina'.

The 'Industrial Enlightenment' as 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002); against Pomeranz, coal and ghost acreage are 'not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job' (2002); found Parthasarathi's case 'simply unpersuasive' (2012). With Kelly and Ó Gráda, labour quality and mechanical skills (2014; 2023).

His exchange with Pomeranz over involution and coal (2002–2003) is drawn on its own arrows and held in economic's dispute strands.

Contested Williams's decline explanation of abolition (1977); writes of 'the Williams-Drescher debate' (1997).

representative_people.works: British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); with Eltis, JEH (2000)

representative_people.works: Empire of Cotton (2014); with Rockman, Slavery’s Capitalism (2016)

representative_people.context: Argued that 'systematized torture' drove cotton productivity and the Industrial Revolution (as Hilt quotes him); The Economist withdrew its review of the book and apologised (2014). Book unread.
representative_people.works: The Half Has Never Been Told (2014)

representative_people.context: An 'ethnography of the Cotton South' (Hilt), who does not count himself a historian of capitalism (Hilt). Book unread.

Co-author with Olmstead of the 2017 paper and 2018 article.

Surveyed ten books of the history of capitalism: 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine these books' effectiveness as social criticism' (2017). He granted that economic research 'casts doubt on some of these arguments and lends support to others', and called for 'dialogue, if not collaboration'.
With Riello, from Atlantic and global history: coercion overstated, US cotton 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution', consumption neglected (2020).
Co-author with Burnard of the 2020 critique of the new history of capitalism.

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term van Nederveen Meerkerk traces to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley doubted whether it described 'successful change at least as much as its cause' (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023, abstract); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage, and the abstract does not name Allen. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong, as Ma's review reports, explained divergence by political scale and war (2011); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.
strands.works: Wong, China Transformed (1997); Frank, ReOrient (1998); Landes, The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Frank's review (2001); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Mokyr (2002; 2012); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.

nodes.label: Robert Brenner
nodes.date_label: “The Civil War Politics of London’s Merchant Community” 1973 · “Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe” 1976 · “The Origins of Capitalist Development” 1977 · “The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism” 1982 · The Brenner Debate (Aston and Philpin, eds) 1985 · Merchants and Revolution 1993 · The Economics of Global Turbulence 1998 (book 2006) · with Christopher Isett, “England’s Divergence from China’s Yangzi Delta” 2002
nodes.description: An American historian of early modern Europe whose 'Agrarian Class Structure and Economic Development in Pre-Industrial Europe' (Past and Present, 1976) opened the Brenner debate. Against the 'demographic model' of Postan and Le Roy Ladurie, and the 'commercialization model' it had displaced, he argued that 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends in the distribution of income and economic growth — and not vice versa'. Similar population trends accompanied serfdom's decline in the West and its rise in the East. English landlords who consolidated holdings and let them to capitalist tenants made agrarian capitalism; in France secure peasant property and the absolutist state blocked it, so that 'the most complete freedom and property rights for the rural population meant poverty'. A companion essay in New Left Review (1977) charged Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism that made trade, not class relations, the motor of development, and acknowledged his 'great debt' to Dobb's critique of Sweezy. Postan and Hatcher (1978) replied that he misrepresented historians who had never given population 'an all-determining role'; Le Roy Ladurie found him 'extremely insular'; Croot and Parker doubted his England–France contrast; the Marxist Guy Bois welcomed the attack on 'the Malthusian model' but called the approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). Brenner's reply (1982) restated the argument as one about 'social-property systems'. Introducing the collected debate (1985), Hilton read it as a continuation of the Dobb–Sweezy transition debate. Merchants and Revolution (1993) gave the English Revolution what Gentles called 'a new social interpretation', centred on London's colonial merchants; later work turned to the postwar world economy (1998) and, with Christopher Isett (2002), answered Pomeranz on England and the Yangzi delta.

nodes.label: Ellen Meiksins Wood
nodes.date_label: “The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism” 1981 · The Retreat from Class 1986 · The Pristine Culture of Capitalism 1991 · Democracy Against Capitalism 1995 · The Origin of Capitalism 1999 (expanded 2002) · “Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism” 2001 · Empire of Capital 2003 · Citizens to Lords 2008 · Liberty and Property 2012
nodes.description: A political theorist and historian, at York University in Toronto from 1967, who became the principal exponent of what Guy Bois, criticising Robert Brenner, had called 'political Marxism'. By the accounts of Alex Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), she accepted the label while rejecting Bois's charge of voluntarism. 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (1981; revised for Democracy Against Capitalism, 1995) argued against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism that Marxism must not perpetuate 'the rigid conceptual separation of the "economic" and the "political"', since capitalism alone draws that line. The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991) turned the Nairn–Anderson theses of a backward Britain around: 'Britain - or rather England - was the world's first capitalist society', and the Continental 'modern' state signalled 'the continuing strength of pre-capitalist social property relations'. She sided there with E. P. Thompson's 'persuasive charge' against an idealised model of bourgeois revolution. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she traced a line from Marx's 'so-called primitive accumulation' through the transition debate, in which Dobb and Hilton 'challenged the commercialization model', to Brenner, who explained 'the emergence of what he calls "market dependence"'. The Origin of Capitalism (1999; expanded 2002) is unread here: its jacket says it challenges accounts that make capitalism's emergence 'seem natural and inevitable', and McAuley (2001) quotes it on 'the naturalization of capitalism, which denies its specificity' (pp. 7–8). Against anti-Eurocentric histories she held that the confusion of commerce with capitalism was itself Eurocentric. Critics called her position 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos), faulted 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for making colonialism marginal (McAuley, after Blaut), and took it to be a caricature of Brenner's (Harman). She answered that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. She also wrote that Christopher Hill's work 'inspired' Brenner's social interpretation of the English Revolution.

Readers and critics: Alex Callinicos (1990); Christopher McAuley (2001); Chris Harman (2004); Robert Brenner (2016); Ken Hirschkop (2016).

Her acceptance of the label 'political Marxism' is reported by Callinicos (1990), Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016); the passage where she accepted it was not read. She is not presented as the originator of the agrarian thesis, which she credited to Marx and Brenner, nor of the label, which was Bois's. Most of her readers and critics named here are Marxist political theorists rather than historians; her relation to historians runs through Brenner, Thompson and Hill. Her work on ancient and early modern political thought (1978–2012) is listed but not surveyed. The debate she joined is held by the group entry capitalismdebates.

edges.relationship: The Dobb–Sweezy transition debate (1950–76) as the first component of the debate on capitalism’s origins
edges.evidence_note: Science & Society 14:2 (1950), read in full: Sweezy's 'root cause … was the growth of trade' (p. 142) against Dobb's 'interaction of the two; although with primary emphasis … upon the internal contradictions' (p. 160). Readers who place it at the head of the line: Hilton (1978, p. 119; 1985, p. 1; Cambridge Core openings); Wood (2001, read): 'the famous Transition Debate which began in 1950 in Science and Society'; Harman (2004 transcript, read): 'The first stage took place in the 1940s and 1950s'. The field strand marx/transition keeps the positions; this arrow records the debate's place in the group entry.

edges.relationship: Feudalism defined by coercive production relations, with trade acting through internal conflicts: the debate’s founding text and reply (1946–50)
edges.evidence_note: Dobb's reply, pp. 158, 160–161, 163, 165 (read): a definition 'advisedly in terms of the relations of production'; trade 'accentuated the internal conflicts'; labour services lasted longest 'in the more advanced south-east'; the seventeenth-century 'ruling class was still feudal'. Sweezy (p. 142): 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Wood (2001) and Harman (1989) treat Dobb as the start of the line Brenner continued. Distinct from edge_319 (Dobb → marx) and edge_479 (Dobb → economic).

edges.relationship: Class structure and property relations as the key to divergent European paths: the Brenner debate (1976–85) and the critique of neo-Smithian Marxism (1977)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (whole article OCRed; p. 31 read closely): 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends … and not vice versa' (p. 31). NLR 1977 (read in transcription): Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein share 'the model put forward by Adam Smith' (§II). The editors' preface (1985, p. vii, Cambridge Core): 'one of the most important historical debates of recent years'. Wood (2001): 'Robert Brenner built on the foundation created by these Marxist historians'.

edges.relationship: Neo-Malthusian, Marxist and regional critics answer Brenner: the demographic historians misrepresented, 'political Marxism', doubtful England–France and east–west contrasts, class struggle narrowed to the countryside (1978–2004)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents the specified interventions of Postan and Hatcher, Le Roy Ladurie, Bois, Croot and Parker and Wunder in Past and Present (1978), and of Harman (1989; 2004) and Callinicos (1990); it is not a verdict of the group entry, which includes Brenner and his supporters. Postan and Hatcher: 'Both imputations are groundless' (p. 64). Le Roy Ladurie: 'somewhat superficial but also extremely insular'; 'simplistic assimilation between power (political) and surplus value (economic)' (pp. 101–102). Croot and Parker: 'Both halves of this argument are suspect' (p. 79). Wunder: 'fallen victim to the Prussian myth' (p. 91). Bois: 'radically disagreeing with his methodological orientation' (p. 107); 'a voluntarist vision of history' (pp. 115–116, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos 1990). Seccombe (1983): a 'tendency to deny the explanatory power of demographic phenomena'. Harman (1989): 'a very narrow view of class struggle'. Concessions kept: Croot and Parker, 'welcome and effective'; Bois, 'courageously attacks the Malthusian model'; Cooper, 'I sympathize with him'; Callinicos, 'a valuable corrective' (p. 111). The 1978 openings are read on Cambridge Core (1985 reprint pages); later pages are not quoted directly; the specified Bois passages (pp. 115–116) are mediated, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990).

edges.relationship: Collects the transition debate (1976) and introduces the Brenner debate as its continuation (1985)

Wood's replies (2002, read) are kept: 'I don't even remotely recognize my argument, or Brenner's'.

edges.relationship: Toynbee's Lectures (1884) define the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations', the concept the later debate revises
edges.evidence_note: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (posthumous, 1884), Saylor transcription without print pages, read by lecture: Lecture I describes 'England on the eve of the Industrial Revolution'; Lecture VIII: 'The essence of the industrial Revolution is the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations which had previously controlled the production and distribution of wealth'; 'The effects of the industrial Revolution prove that free competition may produce wealth without producing well-being.' A reader's warrant: de Vries (1994, p. 249) calls the Industrial Revolution 'By far the most important such monument in economic history'. No claim that Toynbee coined the term or founded the debate; the chain to the 1980s passes through Clapham and Cannadine, unread here.

edges.relationship: Economic historians' measurement and its critics: Crafts and Harley's slower British growth with 'an important discontinuity' reasserted (1992), against Berg and Hudson's case that growth accounting 'mis-specified' the Industrial Revolution (1990/1992)
edges.evidence_note: Crafts and Harley (1992, abstract, read): 'insofar as any adjustment is required the effect is slightly to lower the estimated growth rate … The idea of the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity is reasserted.' Berg and Hudson, working paper (May 1990, read in part): 'the gradualist perspective has appeared to triumph … because of a growing preoccupation with growth accounting' (p. 1); 'N. F. R. Crafts and others may not be able to find the industrial revolution because, in addition to using problematic data, they have mis-specified their subject' (pp. 4–5); 'It is time to move on from the macro accounting framework' (pp. 38–39); 1992 abstract: 'Gradualist perspectives now dominate'. De Vries (1994, pp. 250–251, read) on Lindert and Williamson, Harley and Crafts: 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off," not … pulling down the pillars'. 'Gradualist' is the critics' label; Crafts and Harley reassert a discontinuity.

edges.relationship: Population history in the industrialisation debate: Wrigley turns from population to the 'organic economy' (1988), and Berg and Hudson read Wrigley and Schofield's demographic continuity as 'aggregative' (1990)
edges.evidence_note: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, publisher excerpt): 'After many years spent in work principally concerned with the population history of England, I had returned increasingly to my first main research interest, the better understanding of the industrial revolution' (p. 1); 'My main aim in the lectures was to question the appropriateness of the view that the industrial revolution was a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' (p. 3); the classical economists' writings remain authoritative 'within the confines of … an economy bounded by the productivity of the land, what I shall term an organic economy' (p. 5); coal and steam 'entirely transformed' the prospects for growth (p. 6). The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, p. 3): 'Mining coal provided the solution to this problem.' Berg and Hudson (1990): 'The work of Wrigley and Schofield dominates the population history of this period and illustrates some of the more general problems of causal analysis based on aggregative studies.' Wrigley has no entry in this revision; the arrow is drawn from the field that holds his population work (demography/aggregate_population).
edges.map_label: From population history to the organic economy, 1988–2016

edges.relationship: Household demand as an explanation of industrialisation: de Vries's 'industrious revolution' answers the Crafts–Harley revision (1994) and is extended to 1650–1850 (2008); a reviewer asks whether consumption became a 'deus ex machina' (2009)
edges.evidence_note: De Vries (JEH 1994, pp. 249–251 read): 'The Industrial Revolution as a historical concept has many shortcomings. A new concept—the "industrious revolution"—is proposed to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting … a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon'; he frames it against the revision of 'Peter Lindert and Jeffrey Williamson, Knick Harley, and Nick Crafts' (pp. 250–251). Van Nederveen Meerkerk (TSEG 2009, read in full): Akira Hayami used the term earlier for Japan and 'De Vries adopteerde het begrip'; consumption becomes 'een nieuwe "deus ex machina"' (p. 176). Rosenband (2016, abstract): papermaking raises 'fundamental challenges to this model'. Pomeranz used the concept for Chinese households (2000, p. 17). The household mechanism itself stays on consumption/household_labor and economic/household_demand.

edges.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause: Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment', 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley found that it seemed to describe 'successful change at least as much as its cause' (2010)
edges.evidence_note: Mokyr, 'The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle' (author's draft, October 2002, read pp. 1–4, 10): Enlightenment thinkers 'created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (p. 10). Harley, EH.Net review of Mokyr's book The Enlightened Economy (2009), December 2010 (EH.Net original read, no pages; wording checked 2026-10-18): 'The reader cannot, however, help wondering if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed. The so-called Industrial Enlightenment seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.' The Industrial Enlightenment quotation is from the 2002 draft only; the 2009 book is unread and known here through Harley's review. Mokyr's earlier distinction of invention and adoption stays on technology/invention_adoption. Mokyr has no entry in this revision.

edges.relationship: Pomeranz's reassessment of divergence timing, 2011, as reported by Vries: he 'probably overstated the lateness and suddenness of the Great Divergence', and parity had probably gone by 1750 'if not in 1700'
edges.evidence_note: Vries, Escaping Poverty (2013, p. 17, read), on Pomeranz's 'Ten Years After' (2011, unread): 'the most important Californian, Kenneth Pomeranz, very recently admitted that he probably overstated the lateness and suddenness of the Great Divergence and that economic parity between the two extremes of Eurasia probably had already disappeared in 1750 if not in 1700' (n. 23 cites de Vries's 'after ten years' and Pomeranz's 'Ten years after'). A contribution to the debate's chronology by its principal author, known through one reader's report; a concession, not a critique. Moderate. Pomeranz's 2002–2003 replies concern Huang and stay on edges 1043–1044.

edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison as the California School's method: Wong (1997), Pomeranz (2000) and Parthasarathi's 'parallels in Eurasia' (2011), read by Vries as 'a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians' (2013)
edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz (2000, pp. 7–8, read): a regional approach 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as "deviations" when seen through the expectations of the other'. Parthasarathi (2011, publisher excerpt): earlier explanations 'all identify something that made Europe different … This book takes a different approach … it rejects claims for European difference' (p. 1); 'Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work' (p. 5). Vries (2013, pp. 14–15, read): 'The Californians, moreover, experiment with a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians who not only want to juxtapose but also connect.' The method strands stay on global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources.

edges.relationship: Frank's ReOrient (1998) as the polemical wing of the divergence debate: Asia central until 1800, a debate with Landes announced for December 1998 and an endorsement of Pomeranz (2001)
edges.evidence_note: Notice announcing the Landes–Frank debate (Northeastern University, scheduled for 2 December 1998; read; written from Frank's side; whether the debate took place as announced is not independently confirmed): 'FRANK retorts that … Received social theory … is vitiated by the ingrained EUROCENTRISM of historiography'; Asia 'remained predominant in the world until at 1800'; 'LANDES retorts that Frank and his echoes are a magnet for fallacies and fantasies'. Frank's review of Pomeranz (JAS 2001; author's manuscript read): 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution'; Pomeranz is 'the most important … member of what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'. Mokyr (EH.Net 2012, read): 'The California School, most notably embodied in Kenneth Pomeranz's Great Divergence and Andre Gunder Frank's Re-Orient'. Vries (2013, pp. 15–16) quotes ReOrient (pp. 75, 259) and calls one passage 'a quite silly statement'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 228 n.): Beckert 'is heavily influenced by [world-systems theory's] axioms'. ReOrient itself is unread. Distinct from edge_1053 (Pomeranz → dependency).

edges.relationship: Goldstone's 'efflorescences' of pre-modern growth (2002), and the 'California School' label that readers attribute to him
edges.evidence_note: Goldstone (JWH 2002, abstract): 'many premodern and non-Western economies show spurts or efflorescences of economic growth … Medieval Europe, Golden Age Holland, and Qing China'; the distinctive Western combination 'developed from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries only in Britain'. The label: Frank (2001, read), 'what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'; Vries (2009, p. 35 n. 1, read), 'The term was introduced by Jack Goldstone.' Goldstone's own first use was not found. Vries (2009, p. 48) adds that Californians should 'broaden their approach, as some, e.g. Jack Goldstone, have already done'. Goldstone's earlier comparative work stays on historicalsociology/demographic_crises.

edges.relationship: Capitalism and Slavery (1944) as the starting point of the slavery-and-capitalism component: four arguments taken up and modified by economic historians and by the new history of capitalism
edges.evidence_note: Readers, read: Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 227): 'Four of his arguments are critical to the NHC project: that slavery was central to the Industrial Revolution; that slave wealth was important to the history of eighteenth-century Britain; that the West Indian slave economy went into decline from 1783; and that West Indian slave-owners moved from being a progressive force within mercantilism to being a reactionary force within industrial capitalism'; 'His contemporary defenders, however, use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227); 'a movement among economic historians that accepts a modified version of the Williams thesis' (p. 233). Hilt (JEH 2017, p. 516): 'Like Eric Williams in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), Beckert argues …'; n. 6: Inikori (2002) is 'the strongest recent defense of the Williams hypothesis'. Regele (2023, p. 7): the new work draws on 'a long history of scholarship … most notably Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery'. Pomeranz (2000, p. 3 n. 2): 'the generally negative current mainstream verdicts on the arguments of Eric Williams (1944)'. Distinct from edge_155 (Williams → economic) and edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

edges.relationship: Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers in the making of the Industrial Revolution: Inikori's reassertion of Williams (2002), with the 1987 conference volume on Williams's legacy as its precedent
edges.evidence_note: O'Rourke, EH.Net review of Inikori (2003; read in part): 'His argument is that international trade was crucial to the success of that revolution, in particular trade with the Atlantic Basin (Africa, the West Indies, and the Americas); and that Africans on both sides of the Atlantic were central to this process, both as consumers and producers'; 'a lot of cliometricians will probably conclude that Inikori's argument is not as yet proven'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 227): Inikori is 'Williams' best modern-day defender', concerned that 'the Industrial Revolution owed much more to Africa and Africans than previously thought'. Solow and Engerman (eds, 1987): contents only, with chapters by Solow, Inikori, Richardson and Drescher. Inikori's book itself is unread. Distinct from edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

edges.relationship: Economic historians answer the new history of capitalism: 'fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (Olmstead and Rhode, 2017) and 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning' that 'sometimes undermine' the books (Hilt, 2017); Olmstead and Rhode attribute the observed productivity increase primarily to biological innovation, as Hilt reports
edges.evidence_note: Olmstead and Rhode, AHA paper (programme abstract read; scheduled for 8 January 2017): 'The "New History of Capitalism" grounds the rise of industrial capitalism on the production of raw cotton by American slaves … We show that all make fundamental errors in economic reasoning that affect their major interpretations'; Baptist's torture argument 'is at variance with the ex-slave narratives that he cites and with evidence drawn from plantation records'. Hilt (JEH 2017, read pp. 511–520): 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine these books' effectiveness as social criticism' (p. 511); 'None of the books makes any attempt to falsify major elements of their arguments' (p. 515); on Baptist, Olmstead and Rhode 'show that the increase in productivity they observe was due primarily to biological innovations' (p. 518). Qualification: economic-historical research 'casts doubt on some of these arguments and lends support to others' (p. 516), and Hilt calls for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (p. 511). Hilt reports a measured productivity increase explained primarily by biological innovation; this is not a claim that coercion was absent. The 2018 article is known from metadata only. The earlier Fogel–Engerman debate stays on quant/slavery_debate.

edges.relationship: Class structure, not population or trade, decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth: serfdom in east and west, agrarian capitalism in England against peasant property in France (1976–82)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (whole article OCRed; the quoted pages 31, 47 and 75 read closely): 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends … and not vice versa' (p. 31); the two problems are east–west serfdom and 'the rise of agrarian capitalism and the growth of agricultural productivity in England in relation to their failure in France' (p. 47); 'the most complete freedom and property rights for the rural population meant poverty' (p. 75). Restated in 1982 as 'social-property systems' (Brenner Debate p. 213, Cambridge Core). A contribution within a contested line, not a founding: he writes that the view 'obviously derives from Marx's arguments' (p. 47 n. 40); Postan and Hatcher: 'The essentials of Robert Brenner's argument have been put forward many times before' (1985, p. 64); Cooper: he 'joins a long line of expositors beginning with the Physiocrats' (p. 138).

edges.relationship: Against the 'demographic model' of Postan and its claim to orthodoxy: population substituted for trade as an 'objective variable' that leaves out class structure (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Postan's 'demographic approach' as 'the standard interpretation of long-term socio-economic change in the medieval period' (p. 33); 'what might be termed secular malthusianism has attained something of the level of orthodoxy' (p. 33); 'both Postan and Le Roy Ladurie have chosen to construct new models largely by substituting a different objective variable, population, for the old, discredited one, commerce' (p. 47); 'Postan never really specified the fatal flaw of the trade-centred approach' (p. 43). North and Thomas's contractual view of serfdom is a secondary target (pp. 35–36, 43 n. 32). Hilton (1978, p. 119, Cambridge Core) calls the demographic view 'the prevailing orthodoxy, of which Robert Brenner is simply the latest critic', and Bois (p. 107) also deplores that 'the Malthusian model should have become the orthodox one'. Postan and Hatcher's reply that the charge is 'groundless' is carried by the capitalismdebates → robert_brenner critique.

edges.relationship: Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc cycle read as a Malthusian model that cannot explain why England escaped and France did not (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Le Roy Ladurie's Paysans de Languedoc applied the demographic approach 'rigorously' (p. 33); he quotes 'Malthus came too late' and 'the immense respiration of a social structure' (p. 34); 'Le Roy Ladurie never really poses the question (not only for rural Languedoc but for all of Western Europe) of why the victory of one trend rather than another occurred' (p. 46); 'To explain the failure of agrarian capitalism in France, Le Roy Ladurie falls back, in the last analysis, upon the prevalence of backward mentalities', quoting his 'cultural blockages' (p. 46 n. 37). Le Roy Ladurie's reply (1978) is carried by the capitalismdebates → robert_brenner critique.

edges.relationship: Frank and Wallerstein, with Sweezy before them, charged with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism that makes trade and the division of labour, not class relations, the source of development and underdevelopment (1977)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977), read in full in transcription (no journal pages; by section): 'the basic theoretical underpinnings for the positions set out by all three of these writers is the model put forward by Adam Smith' (§II); with Wallerstein's method 'the rise of trade determines the emergence of capitalists and capitalism; "transition" becomes the result not the source of capitalism' (§VI); Frank's later work has not 'fully broken from the neo-Smithian presuppositions' (§VII); politically, 'the notion of the "development of underdevelopment" opens the way to third-worldist ideology' (Conclusions). Qualified: 'Frank rightly stressed that the expansion of capitalism through trade and investment did not automatically bring with it the capitalist economic development that the Marx of the Manifesto had predicted' (Conclusions). The 1976 essay already cites Wallerstein (1974) as 'a recent version' of the trade explanation of eastern serfdom (p. 53 n. 55). Hilton (1985, p. 1) and Harman (2004 transcript) both name this critique. Brenner thanks Skocpol for her review essay on Wallerstein. A disagreement over method, not a verdict on world-systems research.

edges.relationship: Dobb's critique of Sweezy and his Studies acknowledged as 'of fundamental importance' and a 'great debt' (1977); readers place Brenner in Dobb's line
edges.evidence_note: Brenner's acknowledgement, NLR 1977 n. 11 (read): 'The critique of Sweezy in this exchange by Maurice Dobb, as well as (implicitly) in Dobb's Studies in the Development of Capitalism … is, of course, of fundamental importance—as is Ernesto Laclau's critique of Frank … I hope my great debt to both these writers will be apparent throughout this essay'; Dobb, Studies, pp. 38–42 cited (n. 20). Readers: Hilton (1985, p. 1) calls the debate 'a continuation' of the Dobb–Sweezy debate, and 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978, p. 119) traces the Marxist view of the crisis from Dobb's Studies; Harman (1989, read): 'What Brenner does, essentially, is to take up Dobb's argument, but simplify it'. Harman's own criticism shows the line is not uncritical.

edges.relationship: Reopens the transition from feudalism to capitalism around property relations and class conflict, in the line of the Dobb–Sweezy debate (1976–82)
edges.evidence_note: Hilton (1985, p. 1, Cambridge Core): the debate 'might be regarded as a continuation of that other well-known debate concerning the transition from feudalism to capitalism … sparked off by the criticism by the American economist Paul Sweezy of the analysis given by Maurice Dobb'; that debate 'was largely conducted between Marxists'. Harman (2004 transcript, read) gives 'three distinct stages' of the Marxist debate: Sweezy, Dobb and Hobsbawm; Brenner against Wallerstein and Frank; Pomeranz and Brenner. Brenner's own text locates the problem 'more generally' in 'the transition from feudalism to capitalism' (1976, p. 31). Brenner, at UCLA, is not presented as a member of the British Historians' Group.

edges.relationship: Hilton's studies of serfdom and peasant revolt supply evidence for the 1976 argument; his 1985 introduction frames the debate as a continuation of Dobb–Sweezy
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read) cites Hilton's Decline of Serfdom (pp. 40, 44, 51 notes), 'Rent and Capital Formation' (p. 48 n. 42) and Bond Men Made Free, pp. 114–15, 125–73 (p. 56 n. 64) for commutation, seigneurial reaction and peasant revolt. Hilton framed the collected debate (introduction, p. 1, Cambridge Core). In 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978; 1985 p. 119, Cambridge Core opening) he called Brenner 'simply the latest critic' of the demographic orthodoxy, and traced the Marxist view from Dobb's Studies through the transition debate to Bois's Crise du féodalisme. Evidence and editorial framing, not an influence on Brenner's theory.

edges.relationship: Tawney's Agrarian Problem supplies the evidence on entry fines for the English case (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Tawney's Agrarian Problem among the works 'On English agrarian change' (p. 42 n. 30); on fines at will as the landlords' lever, 'Tawney, Agrarian Problem, pp. 287–310', pp. 296–300, 307 (p. 62 nn. 76, 78). Evidence, not an acknowledged framework. Ormrod's 'Agrarian Capitalism and Merchant Capitalism: Tawney, Dobb, Brenner and Beyond' (2013) is located but unread; read it before any upgrade to influence.

edges.relationship: With Isett, the divergence of England and the Yangzi delta traced to different social-property relations already in place, not to coal and colonies (2002)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner and Isett, JAS 61:2 (2002): 609–662. Opening read (Cambridge extract): 'Kenneth Pomeranz (2000) proposes a radical revision … by as late as 1800, there was little to choose between them'. Opening sections read for revision 1.144 in the International Socialism repost (no JAS pages): 'the institutional framework or system of social-property relations that structured the English economy was radically different … from that of the Yangzi delta'; 'It was this already existing decisive divergence, not England's capacity to gain access to the American colonies … that explains why the two economies distanced themselves'; the delta followed 'a Malthusian pattern', England 'a Smithian pattern'; 'Contra Pomeranz'. Moved here from edge_1050 in revision 1.145, as that edge's note foresaw. Same JAS issue as Huang's critique and Pomeranz's reply. A later and smaller dispute than the 1976–85 debate.

edges.relationship: Marx's account of 'so-called primitive accumulation' named as the source of the view (1976)
edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976, p. 47 n. 40 (read): 'This view obviously derives from Marx's arguments on the barriers to and the class structural bases for the development of capitalism, especially as presented in "The So-called Primitive Accumulation of Capital", Capital, i, pt. VIII, and Pre-Capitalist Economic Formations'. In 2004 he argued against Marx's Preface model of the productive forces (transcript, read), so the debt is selective.

edges.relationship: Hill's revisions of the 'bourgeois revolution' read as the inspiration for Brenner's 'another social interpretation' of the English Revolution (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Wood, 'Christopher Hill and the Recovery of History' (Against the Current, 2003, read in full): 'Other Marxists, notably Robert Brenner, have developed another social interpretation … (See especially the Conclusion to Brenner's Merchants and Revolution …) It hardly needs saying that Hill's pioneering work has inspired these fruitful developments in Marxist historiography.' Gentles (NLR, 1994, opening): Brenner wrote 'in spite of his great admiration for the work of Christopher Hill and Lawrence Stone'. Two readers' explicit claims; Brenner's own acknowledgement is unread because the book is unread. Moderate.

edges.relationship: Brenner's account of agrarian social-property relations and 'market dependence' as the foundation of her origin of capitalism (1981–2002)
edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements and uses: 1981 n. * thanks Brenner, and n. 14 cites his NLR essay (Verso repost, read). In 2001 (read): 'Robert Brenner built on the foundation created by these Marxist historians … what he calls "market dependence"'. In 2002 (read): capitalism has '"rules for reproduction" (to use Brenner's term)'. Readers: McAuley (2001), 'she admittedly draws on Robert Brenner's findings and conclusions'; Callinicos (1990), 'Wood's employment of his work to construct "political Marxism"' (p. 112); Brenner (2016) on their friendship from 1978. An exchange between them on the Low Countries (Journal of Agrarian Change, 2001–02) is listed bibliographically and unexamined here.

edges.relationship: Against Cohen's technological determinism: the 'material base' is social and historical, and the separation of the economic from the political is specific to capitalism (1981)
edges.evidence_note: Verso repost of NLR I/127 (read in part): Cohen's book is used 'to support an argument against a social interpretation of materialism'; 'what Cohen's technological determinism does is to repeat the error of the political economists: he generalizes the particular historical experience of capitalism'. Callinicos (1990, read): this 'is by no means the first time that Wood has used Brenner's work to distinguish her alternative reading of historical materialism from Cohen's' (p. 111). Brenner (2016): 'Here Ellen's main target was … Gerald Cohen'.

edges.relationship: Thompson's critique of the Nairn–Anderson theses, adopted in her account of English capitalism (1991)
edges.evidence_note: Pristine Culture (1991, publisher extract, read): her preferred thesis 'is more compatible with arguments put forward by E.P. Thompson in the original debate, and less subject to his persuasive charge that Nairn-Anderson operated with an abstractly idealized model of a "Bourgeois Revolution"'. Democracy Against Capitalism ch. 2 (1995, Cambridge Core opening): anyone '(like E.P. Thompson) working somewhere in the fissures … is likely to be badly misunderstood'. 2001 (read): 'Like other Marxist historians such as E.P. Thompson, Brenner understands industrialization …'. Hirschkop (2016): 'The prominence of historians within this group (Edward Thompson and John Saville among others) was probably decisive'. Thompson's 'Peculiarities of the English' is not in the graph and unread here.

edges.relationship: Anti-Eurocentric histories (Frank's Asian-centred world economy, Blaut's 'protocapitalism') said to share the Eurocentric confusion of commerce with capitalism (2001)
edges.evidence_note: 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001, read): the critiques 'deny the "superiority" of Europe and emphasize … the dominance, of non-European economies and trading networks' (for example 'Andre Gunder Frank's argument about the Asian-dominated world'). Since Blaut 'does not conceive of capitalism as a specific social form, he can have no clear conception of non- or precapitalist modes of production'. McAuley's reply (2001) and her rejoinders (2002) are recorded on the capitalismdebates → ellen_meiksins_wood critique. Frank's later Asia-centred work is outside the dependency strands, so this is a critique of the tradition's later turn, not of the 1966 hypotheses.

edge_1050.relationship: Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe's stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Mokyr finds coal and ghost acreage 'not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job' (2002); Vries finds differences, not 'surprising resemblances' (2009); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
edge_1050.map_label: Knowledge, wages, the state and regional GDP, 2002–2021
edge_1050.evidence_note: This arrow represents named interventions within the debate entry, not a verdict of it; the entry includes Pomeranz and his allies, and each intervention establishes something different. Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Mokyr ('The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle', author's draft, October 2002, pp. 2–4 read), on knowledge: of coal, 'the argument can be and has been overdone'; of ghost acreage, 'this argument is not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job'; Pomeranz 'does not confront the "Needham Questions" squarely'; 'the sheer enormity of the gap requires a better explanation than historical luck (European discoveries) or geographical accident (coal, proximity to America)'. Vries ('A World of Surprising Resemblances?', 2009, pp. 35–38, 47–48 read), on agriculture and the state: 'I would not call that a "surprising resemblance"' (p. 38); 'Coal and colonies definitely were fundamental in the Rise of the West. But reference to them cannot suffice to explain it' (p. 48). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: 'our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England'; 'Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism' (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the 'rise of the west' literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: 'The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers' (p. 958); the qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates, and moved Brenner and Isett's 2002 critique to its own arrow (robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz), as this note had foreseen.

edge_407.relationship: Drescher contests the economic-decline explanation for 1807 abolition (1977, in the publisher's description of Econocide); Eltis and Engerman judge the growth linkages of slavery to British industry small (2000, as Hilt reports)
edge_407.map_label: Decline and abolition disputed; slavery’s weight questioned, 1977–2000
edge_407.evidence_note: In its publisher's description (the monograph is unread), Econocide (1977) emphasizes continued economic potential and public mobilization. This is one named intervention within economic/abolition debates, not the entire field’s verdict or a test of all Williams’s propositions. Full statistical evidence remains unchecked. The arrow concerns the decline-and-abolition and growth-linkage questions; slave-derived wealth in British society is carried by Hall's edges. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates and added further named readers. Drescher's own retrospect ('Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years', 1997, opening read) names 'the Williams-Drescher debate' and calls the book 'a classic' that reoriented the subject. Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000, unread; mediated) concluded, as Hilt reports (JEH 2017, p. 516), that 'the total value added and growth-inducing linkages of the British slave trade and Caribbean slave plantations were not particularly large'; Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 226) quote Solow's middle position, that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (1987, p. 72), and judge that Williams's 'contemporary defenders … use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227).

edge_478.evidence_note: Sweezy pp. 134–137 questions breadth and regional transfer; Takahashi pp. 313–315 calls for fuller French/German engagement while developing production-relation analysis. Two distinct interventions, not a united school or complete reading of both critiques. Revision 1.145: Sweezy's critique, now read in full (pp. 134–157), was offered as a correction from within: 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct' (p. 142); his own model made feudalism 'a system of production for use' (p. 136) and the growth of trade 'the root cause' of its decline (p. 142).

edge_899.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz, which revision 1.145 moved to capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz, with Brenner and Isett drawn separately as robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

row.context: Class structure and property relations, not population or trade, explain divergent agrarian paths in England, France and eastern Europe; against the demographic model of Postan (1976–82).
row.works: "Agrarian Class Structure" (1976); "The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism" (1982)

row.context: An American Marxist historian whose 1976 article Hilton (1985) read as a continuation of the Dobb–Sweezy transition debate; acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb (1977). Not a member of the British Historians' Group.
Charged Frank and Wallerstein, with Sweezy, with a 'neo-Smithian' Marxism (1977), while crediting Frank's break with stage theory.
Criticised Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc cycle as a demographic model that never asks why one trend won; Le Roy Ladurie replied (1978). Exchange, not membership.
row.works: Past and Present (1976); reply by Le Roy Ladurie (1978)

row.context: Comparative analysis of agrarian property relations; Callinicos (1994) places the work 'within the canon of what has come to be known as historical sociology'.
With Isett (2002), answered Pomeranz that England and the Yangzi delta already differed in social-property relations. Later and smaller than the 1976–85 debate.
Against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism: Marxism must not perpetuate 'the rigid conceptual separation of the "economic" and the "political"' (1981; 1995).

A reader of the Historians' Group: she traced Hill's move from an orthodox 'bourgeois revolution' and placed Dobb and Hilton at the start of the line Brenner continued (2001, 2003). Not a member of the British group.
row.works: "Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism" (2001); "Christopher Hill and the Recovery of History" (2003)
